title: Agitation
diagnosis: Possible neuropsychiatric disorders such as delirium, dementia, or psychiatric emergencies
correct_orders: Obtain vital signs, perform a detailed physical examination, and assess mental status
Order laboratory workup: CBC, electrolytes, glucose, renal/hepatic function tests, thyroid function tests, urine toxicology screen
Order imaging studies if necessary (CT scan or MRI of the brain)
Consult psychiatry for further evaluation and management
Consider voluntary hospitalization — if the patient poses a risk to self or others, escalate to involuntary psychiatric hold
should_avoid: Prescribe medications without a clear diagnosis (e.g., antipsychotics, benzodiazepines)

rationale.Obtain vital signs, perform a detailed p: To gather initial data on the patient's condition
rationale.Order laboratory workup: To help rule out medical causes of agitation such as electrolyte imbalances, infections, or metabolic disorders
rationale.Order imaging studies: If necessary to further evaluate potential neurological conditions
rationale.Consult psychiatry: For a comprehensive evaluation and management plan
rationale.Consider voluntary hospitalization — if: To determine the appropriate level of care and ensure patient safety
rationale.Prescribe medications without a clear di: Could lead to incorrect treatment and potential harm due to lack of proper diagnostics
rationale.CMP / BMP: To evaluate electrolytes, renal and liver function which could contribute to the patient's agitation
rationale.UA: To rule out urinary tract infection or other kidney-related issues

physical_exam: Agitation — exam tailored to chief complaint on arrival.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
No acute rash; capillary refill and perfusion assessed.
